DRY LAB
 CORONARY CIRCULATION




     OBJECTIVES
Describe the coronary circulation and
explain how it supplies the myocardium.
Identify the right and left coronary arteries,
their origins, courses, major branches and
areas of supply.
Identify the main cardiac veins and explain
how they drain into the coronary sinus or
directly into the right atrium.
Recognise key coronary vessels on anterior
and posterior views of the heart and on
coronary angiograms.
Use the course of a vessel and the sulcus it
occupies to distinguish the major arteries
and veins during practical identification

1. Overview of coronary circulation
Coronary circulation is the blood supply to the myocardium (heart
muscle). The heart needs its own circulation because the blood inside
the chambers does not directly supply the thick muscular wall
adequately. The main arterial supply comes from the right coronary
artery (RCA) and left coronary artery (LCA), which arise from the
aorta. Venous blood is collected by the cardiac veins and returned
mainly to the right atrium through the coronary sinus.
                        →         →
• Arterial side: right and left coronary arteries   smaller branches
capillaries in the myocardium.
               →            →
• Venous side: cardiac veins   mainly coronary sinus   right atrium.
• Important exception: the anterior cardiac veins open directly into
the right atrium, and the smallest cardiac veins drain directly into the
heart chambers.
(Learn the vessels together with the surface/sulcus they occupy.)

2. Right coronary artery (RCA)
Practical identification: On an anterior view, look for the RCA
arising from the right aortic sinus and running in the right
AV/coronary sulcus. The right marginal branch follows the
acute margin. The PDA is identified on the posterior surface in
the posterior interventricular sulcus.


Origin and course
• Origin: right aortic (coronary) sinus of the ascending aorta.
• The RCA passes anteriorly, b/w the right atrial appendage (right
auricle) and the pulmonary trunk.
• It then descends in the coronary sulcus, also called the
atrioventricular (AV) groove, b/w the right atrium and right ventricle.
• It curves around to the posterior/diaphragmatic surface of the heart
on the right.
Major branches
• Atrial branches, including the sinoatrial (SA) nodal branch. The SA
nodal branch supplies the SA node, the usual pacemaker of the heart.
• Anterior atrial and ventricular branches, which supply parts of the
right atrium and right ventricle.
• Right (acute) marginal branch, which follows the acute/right margin
of the heart and supplies the right ventricle.
• AV nodal branch, commonly arising as the RCA courses along the
diaphragmatic surface; it supplies the atrioventricular node.
• Posterior interventricular artery (posterior descending artery, PDA),
usually the final major branch in the right-dominant pattern. It runs in
the posterior interventricular sulcus.
Distribution/areas supplied
• Most of the right atrium and right ventricle.
• The posterior 1/3rd of the interventricular septum, usually via the
posterior interventricular artery.

3. Left coronary artery (LCA)


Practical identification: The LAD is the artery in the anterior
interventricular sulcus. The circumflex follows the coronary sulcus
on the left side and curves towards the posterior surface. Do not
confuse the coronary sulcus with the interventricular sulci.


Origin and course
• Origin: left aortic (coronary) sinus.
• The short main stem passes between the pulmonary trunk and the left
atrial appendage (left auricle).
• Behind the pulmonary trunk, it divides into two main terminal branches:
the anterior interventricular artery (LAD) and the circumflex artery.
Major branches
• Anterior interventricular artery (left anterior descending artery, LAD):
descends in the anterior interventricular sulcus towards the apex. It gives
diagonal branches and septal/interventricular branches.
• Circumflex artery: turns left and follows the coronary sulcus around the
left side of the heart. It gives branches to the left atrium and left ventricle;
a left/obtuse marginal branch may arise from it.
Distribution/areas supplied
• Most of the left ventricle.
• A small part of the right ventricle.
• Most of the left atrium.
• The anterior two-thirds of the interventricular septum, mainly through
LAD septal branches.
• Distal parts of the conducting system.
X-RAY IDENTIFICATION

4. Coronary dominance
Coronary dominance is defined by which coronary artery gives rise to the
posterior interventricular artery (PDA), not simply by which coronary artery
is larger.
• Right-dominant circulation: the PDA arises from the RCA. This is the most
common pattern.
• Left-dominant circulation: the PDA arises from the circumflex branch of the
LCA. This is less common.
• The artery that supplies the SA node can vary: it arises from the RCA in
most cases, but from the LCA/circumflex system in a substantial minority.
(For dominance, trace the origin of the PDA. “Right coronary artery is
larger” is not the definition of right dominance.)
Auricle

5. Cardiac veins and the coronary sinus
Cardiac veins generally accompany coronary arteries, but their names are
not always identical to the arteries they accompany. Most venous blood
from the myocardium drains into the coronary sinus.
Coronary sinus
• A large venous channel on the posterior aspect of the heart, in the
coronary sulcus.
• Receives most of the cardiac venous blood.
• Opens into the right atrium.
Major tributaries / cardiac veins
1. Great cardiac vein
• Begins near the apex and ascends with the LAD in the anterior
interventricular sulcus.
• Turns left at the coronary sulcus and accompanies the circumflex artery
towards the back of the heart.
• Enlarges in the posterior coronary sulcus to continue as the coronary
sinus.
• Drains the anterior aspects of the right and left ventricles and the
interventricular septum.
2. Middle cardiac vein
• Begins near the apex and ascends in the posterior interventricular sulcus
with the posterior interventricular artery (PDA).
• Opens into the coronary sinus.
• Drains the posterior/diaphragmatic aspects of both ventricles and the
interventricular septum.
3. Small cardiac vein
• Begins as the right marginal vein and follows the right margin of the
heart.
• Drains parts of the right side of the right ventricle.
• Usually opens into the coronary sinus.

4. Posterior cardiac vein (posterior vein of the left ventricle)
• Runs on the posterior surface of the left ventricle, to the left of the middle
cardiac vein.
• Drains the posterior aspect of the left ventricle and opens into the coronary
sinus.
5. Anterior cardiac veins
• Small veins on the anterior surface of the right ventricle.
• Cross the coronary sulcus and drain directly into the right atrium rather
than into the coronary sinus.
6. Thebesian veins
• The smallest cardiac veins.
• Drain directly into the chambers of the heart.

6. Vessel identification by surface and sulcus





7. Coronary angiograms shown in the lecture
• An angiogram displays the coronary arterial tree after contrast has been
introduced into the vessels.
• In a right coronary angiogram, trace the vessel from its origin and follow
its course around the right side of the heart; identify the right marginal and
posterior interventricular branches where visible.
• In a left coronary angiogram, identify the short LCA stem and its division
into LAD and circumflex branches.
• Use the branching pattern and course to identify the vessel; do not rely
only on the orientation of the image, because radiographic views can differ.
• How to approach a specimen or image: First orient the heart (anterior vs
posterior surface), then find the sulcus, then trace the vessel. Finally, name
the vessel and state one structure/region it supplies or drains.

WET LAB
INTERNAL FEATURES OF THE HEART




       OBJECTIVES



     Identify the internal features of the Right and
     Left atrium and Ventricles
     Identify the features of the AV and Semilunar
    Valves
     Identify the featues of the interventricular
    septum, interatrial septum and the fossa
     ovalis

1.Right atrium

 Lined by the pectinate muscles
 Superiorly terminate in the crista terminalis which appears as a
ridge
 SA node is found in the top right of crista terminalis
 Fossa ovalis which is formed after fusion of foramen ovale after
birth appears as a thinner membranous structure compared to its
surroundings
 Failure of its formation leads to atrial septal defect
 Eustachian valve of superior vena cava and Thebesian valve of
coronary sinus is observed near their respective blood vessels:
They Receives blood from venae cavae and releases it into right
ventricle

2. Right ventricle

 Forms most of sternocostal surface
 Inflow of blood from the right atrium through rough trabeculae
carneae
 Outflow through the smooth infundibulum (conus arteriosus),
pulmonary semilunar valve and pulmonary artery
 Atrium and ventricle separated by tricuspid valve
 Anchored by papillary muscles (anterior, posterior and septal) which
anchor the chordae tendineae
 Moderator band of septomarginal trabecula which carries conductive
tissue right bundle branch (electrical support) and prevents over-
distention of ventricle (mechanical support)

3. Left atrium
Forms most of the base
Receives blood from the four pulmonary veins
Outflow- through the mitral valve into the left ventricle
Pectinate muscles are mainly found in auricle
Most common site of atrial fibrosis

              4. Left ventricle
Has the thickest muscle wall among all chambers
About 2-3x thicker than right ventricle
Has finer trabeculae carneae than RV
Inflow of blood through the left atrium and mitral valve
Outflow through aortic vestibule (smooth outlet), semilunar valves and aorta

5. Inter-ventricular septum
 Made of 1/3 membranous part, which is the most common site of
septal defect in congenital heart disease
 Av bundle runs along lower border of it
 2/3 muscular part, which is thick and forms most of septum

           6. Atrio-ventricular valves
 Bicuspid/ tricuspid
 Anchored by chordae tendineae which are pulled by papillary muscles
when they contract
 Close when ventricles are contracting

              7. Semilunar valves
 Operate on pressure difference between ventricles and blood vessels
 Lack chordae tendinea or papillary muscles
 Both are tricuspid
 Pocket like cusps, each present with a central nodule
 Cusps in aortic valve have coronary ostia (holes) that supply the
coronary arteries (left and right respectively)
 Aortic valve cusps- left, right, posterior
 Pulmonary valve cusps- left, right, anterior

HISTO LAB
HISTOLOGY OF ARTERIES AND VEINS




     OBJECTIVES

 Identify the three tunics of blood vessels: tunica
 intima, tunica media, and tunica externa
 Identify and distinguish: elastic artery, muscular
 artery, small muscular artery, arteriole, capillary,
venule, and vein
 Identify elastic lamellae, internal elastic lamina (IEL),
and external elastic lamina (EEL)
 Distinguish arteries from veins based on wall
 thickness, lumen shape, and tunica organization
 Identify longitudinal smooth muscle bundles and
collagen fibers in large veins such as the SVC
 Identify capillaries by their endothelial wall and red
blood cells passing through the lumen

1. General Structure of 3 tunic/layers
1) Tunica intima
   endothelium (simple squamous)
   basement membrane
   subendothelial connective tissue + fibroblasts

2) Tunica media (no fibroblasts present)
   fenestrated elastic lamellae
   contains Vascular Smooth Muscle Cells
Function of VSMC: contraction + synthesis of collagen
and ground matrix (behaving like fibroblasts)

3) Tunica externa
   contains Elactic fibres and Collagen
   Fibroblasts and macrophages





 Artery
1) Tunica intima: thin
2) Tunica media: thick (more VSMC + elastic tissue)
3) Tunica externa: thin
Lumen: rounder in shape due to a thicker tunica media
hence more smooth muscle

 Vein
1) Tunica intima: thin
2) Tunica media: thin (less VSMC + elastic tissue)
3) Tunica externa: thick
Lumen: more oval/irregular in shape due to a thinner tunica
media hence less smooth muscle (more collapsed)

Types of arteries:

             1) Large elastic artery

 Tunica intima: endothelium + BM + subendothelial connective tissue

 Tunica media: thickest layer (no fibroblasts)
  1. Many concentric elastic lamellae (70 layers) (shown by arrow)
 2. Circular vascular smooth muscle cells (40 layers) (shown by arrow)

 Tunica externa: collagen and elastic fibres; fibroblasts and
macrophage; vasa vasorum and nervi vasorum

 Example: aorta
  Functional name: conducting artery





         Using special stain:

                         1 is concentric elastic lamella
              2 is smooth muscle cells

2) Medium Muscular Artery

       Less wavy fenestrated elastic lamellae (2 layers: IEL+EEL)
      More smooth muscle (20 layers)
       Tunica intima: endothelium + BM + subendothelial connective tissue
     + fibroblasts
       Tunica media: Circular smooth muscle cells + collagen
       Tunica externa: CT (collagen + elastic fibres + fibroblasts)
         IEL: internal elastic lamina found between tunica intima and
   tunica media
        EEL: external elastic lamina found between tunica media and
   tunica externa
      Another way to think of IEL & EEL is that they are the borders of
      tunica media
      Example: ulnar artery
       Functional name: distributing artery





    Small muscular artery + its accompanying small
                  muscular vein
 Artery: 1 wavy fenestrated elastic lamellae
( IEL ) + 10 smooth muscle layers
 Vein: no elastic lamina + less smooth
muscle
 Example: digital arteries
 Functional name: small distributing artery

3) Arteriole + its accompanying Muscular Venule

  Vasa vasorum = blood vessels of blood vessels
   Function: supplying walls of larger blood vessels with oxygen +
  nutrients
  Hence located mainly in the outermost layer of vessel (tunica
 externa) as innermost layer (tunica intima) is already in contact
 with blood
  NOTE: not all arterioles are vasa vasorum; only those who supply
 walls of large vessels

   Arteriole: rounder lumen, thicker wall than the venule, bulgy
 nucleus
   Tunica intima: endothelium + BM + thin subendothelial connective
  tissue
   Tunica media: 1-2 layer of circular smooth muscle
   Tunica externa: thin layer of CT
  NO IEL (internal elastic lamina)

  Muscular venule: collapsed and more oval lumen, thinner wall
 than the arteriole, flat nucleus
   Tunica intima: endothelium + BM + subendothelial connective
  tissue
   Tunica media: 1-2 layers of circular smooth muscle +
 NO elastic fibres
   Tunica externa: thin layer of CT

Capillary in human tongue:

    Only 1 tunic present : tunica intima
    Tunica intima: endothelium + BM
   No tunica media nor tunica externa
   No smooth muscle present
    Very narrow lumen
     Function: main site of gas exchange





        Large Veins: SVC & IVC

1) Tunica intima: endothelium + BM +
subendothelial
connective tissue + fibroblasts
2) Tunica media: thin; few circular smooth
muscle layers + collagen

3) Tunica externa: thickest; containing collagen fibres (bright red/pink)
              - AND Thick longitudinal smooth muscle bundles
                        (dark red circles)





         FUNCTION: prevent collapse of vein when blood
                       volume is low
        NOTE: the thick longitudinal smooth muscle bundles
                     are mainly found in IVC

HISTO LAB QUESTIONS

 Question 1.
 A) Identify the type of blood vessel shown.
 B) Give one identification point.





 Answers:
 A) Elastic artery
 B) Many fenestrated elastic laminae in the tunica media


Question 2.
What type of cell is marked by the arrow and what type of
blood vessel is this?





Answer:
The blood vessel is an arteriole. The identification point is the
absence of elastic laminae in the tunica media and the presence of
a single smooth muscle layer in the tunica media.

Question 3.
(1) What is the tissue the arrow is pointing at?
(2) Where would you find it?
(3) What cell makes it?





Answer:
(1) Inner Elastic Lamina
(2) Tunica Intima
(3) Fibroblasts

Question 4.
(1) What vessel is the red arrow pointing at (2) What vessel is the
green arrows pointing at? (3) What vessel is the yellow arrow
pointing at?





Answers:
(1) Lymphatic capillary
(2) Venule
(3) Arteriole

WET LAB QUESTIONS


Question 1.
A. Label the marked structure
B. Give 2 arteries that supply it





Answer:
A. Interventicular septum
B. Left anterior descending (anterior ⅓) and posterior
interventricular artery
(posterior ⅔)


Question 2.
A. What is X and Y
B. What is the function of Y?



Answer:
A. X is Chordae Tendineae
& Y is Papillary muscle
B. Stabilizes the cusps

Question 3.
(A)Identify structure 2 and explain
how it forms
(B) Identify structure 3
(C) Identify structure 1
Answer:
(A) Fossa ovalis, the remnant of
the foramen ovale and forms due to
the left atrial pressure, causing the
septum primum and septum
secundum to fuse. The fossa ovalis
is characterised by minimal
thickness hence can be determined
via transillumination
(B) Pectinate muscles
(C) Crista terminalis; exteriorly it’s
called the sulcus terminalis



Question 4.
Identify structures A and D and
state the function of structure A

Answers:
A) Moderator (septomarginal)
band. It contains right bundle
branch and conducts action
potential, ensuring that the right
ventricle contracts at the same
time as the left ventricle, ensuring
synchronous ejection.

Dr. Osama also stated that it allows a slightly faster depolarisation of
the right ventricle compared to the left ventricle.
D) Papillary muscle: These muscles contract to tighten chordae
tendineae and prevent valve prolapse during ventricular systole.
